verses.text: Woe to you who destroy, but you weren’t destroyed; and who betray, but nobody betrayed you! When you have finished destroying, you will be destroyed; and when you have finished betrayal, you will be betrayed.
Yahweh, be gracious to us. We have waited for you. Be our strength every morning, our salvation also in the time of trouble.
At the noise of the thunder, the peoples have fled. When you lift yourself up, the nations are scattered.
Your plunder will be gathered as the caterpillar gathers. Men will leap on it as locusts leap.
Yahweh is exalted, for he dwells on high. He has filled Zion with justice and righteousness.
There will be stability in your times, abundance of salvation, wisdom, and knowledge. The fear of Yahweh is your treasure.
Behold, their valiant ones cry outside; the ambassadors of peace weep bitterly.
The highways are desolate. The traveling man ceases. The covenant is broken. He has despised the cities. He doesn’t respect man.
The land mourns and languishes. Lebanon is confounded and withers away. Sharon is like a desert, and Bashan and Carmel are stripped bare.
“Now I will arise,” says Yahweh; “Now I will lift myself up. Now I will be exalted.
You will conceive chaff. You will give birth to stubble. Your breath is a fire that will devour you.
The peoples will be like the burning of lime, like thorns that are cut down and burned in the fire.
Hear, you who are far off, what I have done; and, you who are near, acknowledge my might.”
The sinners in Zion are afraid. Trembling has seized the godless ones. Who among us can live with the devouring fire? Who among us can live with everlasting burning?

He who walks righteously, and speaks blamelessly; He who despises the gain of oppressions, who gestures with his hands, refusing to take a bribe, who stops his ears from hearing of blood, and shuts his eyes from looking at evil —
he will dwell on high. His place of defense will be the fortress of rocks. His bread will be supplied. His waters will be sure.
Your eyes will see the king in his beauty. They will see a distant land.
Your heart will meditate on the terror. Where is he who counted? Where is he who weighed? Where is he who counted the towers?
You will no longer see the fierce people, a people of a deep speech that you can’t comprehend, with a strange language that you can’t understand.

Look at Zion, the city of our appointed festivals. Your eyes will see Jerusalem, a quiet habitation, a tent that won’t be removed. Its stakes will never be plucked up, nor will any of its cords be broken.
But there Yahweh will be with us in majesty, a place of wide rivers and streams, in which no galley with oars will go, neither will any gallant ship pass by there.
For Yahweh is our judge. Yahweh is our lawgiver. Yahweh is our king. He will save us.
Your rigging is untied. They couldn’t strengthen the foot of their mast. They couldn’t spread the sail. Then the prey of a great plunder was divided. The lame took the prey.
The inhabitant won’t say, “I am sick.” The people who dwell therein will be forgiven their iniquity.

footnotes.content: The destroyer who hasn't been destroyed yet—there's a warning wrapped in this verse. Evil has a habit of thinking itself exempt, believing it can keep plundering forever. But the Lord sees every act of violence and betrayal, and His justice is neither forgetful nor rushed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Notice how Israel petitions: not "Be great," but "Be our strength, every morning." They ask for what they need when they need it. This is prayer lived day by day, not once and for all—a humble knowing that grace renews with each dawn.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Thunder—the voice of God's power breaking through. Nations don't scatter because they've thought their way there; they flee because they hear and see the Lord Himself exalted. His lifting up is irresistible; it commands respect that no argument could.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The plunder of the wicked gathers up like chaff—easy to collect, easy to scatter. What the destroyer gathered so proudly becomes carrion-food for insects. There's a quiet justice in how the Lord turns theft into nothing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zion filled with justice and righteousness—this is what the Lord actually builds on. He doesn't shore up Zion by making it richer or more defended; He establishes it by filling it with His own character. That's an unshakable foundation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Stability, abundance, wisdom, knowledge, fear of the Lord—the verse stacks these treasures like a chest for Zion. But notice what holds the deepest value: the fear of Yahweh. Everything else follows from a right relationship with Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The strong cry outside, the peacemakers weep bitterly. Even the mighty are undone; even diplomacy fails. In that despair, there's nowhere left to turn—except up, to the God who alone can break the deadlock.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When the covenant is broken, the land itself suffers. Roads empty. Cities crumble. The loss is total because breaking faith with God isn't just a spiritual slip—it's a rupture that touches everything a people has built.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Lebanon withers, Sharon becomes desert, Carmel is stripped bare—three fertile lands emptied of their greenness. This isn't poetry only; it's real devastation. The Lord shows what judgment looks like written across the landscape.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Now I will arise"—after all the desolation, the turning point comes with God's own word. He's not been passive; He's waited for the right moment. His rising up is both vindication for the faithful and reversal for the proud.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The wicked conceive chaff and give birth to stubble—their schemes are empty from the start. And their own schemes devour them, like breathing fire into one's own lungs. Sin is its own executioner.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peoples burned like lime and thorns—the comparison is brutal and plain. But notice that the Lord is the fire doing the burning. This isn't chaos; it's judgment, clear and purposeful.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Hear, you who are far off; you who are near, acknowledge"—the Lord calls both distant and near to witness His work. None are excused. His mighty acts speak to all creation, demanding recognition.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The sinners are terrified; the godless tremble. But here's the real question posed: "Who can live with everlasting burning?" It's not boasting—it's a threshold question. Only the righteous can stand before His holiness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The portrait here is exact: walks righteously, speaks truly, refuses bribes, stops ears from blood-talk, shuts eyes from evil. This isn't theoretical righteousness—it's the daily discipline of someone who has chosen the Lord's way in concrete choices.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The righteous dwells on high. His supply is sure. Bread, water, fortress—God covers the basics. Doesn't mean luxury, but it means trustworthy provision. The Lord sustains those who hold His way.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The eyes of the faithful see the king in his beauty. Not the earthly throne, but the Lord Himself—revealed, resplendent, undeniable. And they see a distant land, the inheritance not yet in hand but promised and secure.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The heart no longer meditates on terror; no longer counts the enemy's strength, weighs their towers, plans defense. All that fearful mathematics vanishes when the Lord is exalted. Peace replaces the exhaustion of worry.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The fierce people—the ones whose hard speech confuses and whose strange tongue bewilders—they're gone from sight. The immediate threat dissolves. The Lord didn't answer by granting wisdom to understand the enemy; He answered by removing them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zion described as a tent—temporary-looking, yet unremoved. Appointed festivals gathered there. This is home: simple, quiet, stable. The image promises that God's dwelling-place with His people will endure, even when it seems fragile.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Wide rivers and streams surround Zion—a picture of abundance and beauty. But no galley will sail there, no warrior-ship will pass. The place of God is protected by more than walls; it's preserved by the Lord's will.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh is judge, lawgiver, king—all power flows from His throne. In one verse, the entire structure of justice and rule is revealed as centered in the Lord alone. He will save us. All roles converge in His person.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The enemy ship falls apart—rigging untied, mast unsecured, sail spread uselessly. Their plunder scatters, and even the lame can gather it. Defeat is so complete that the weakest scavenge what the mighty abandoned.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo of this promise: no inhabitant says "I am sick," and all iniquity is forgiven. In Christ, that healing and that forgiveness have arrived. The Lord who promised Zion's restoration has opened the way for all who believe to dwell in it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
